title: What Lurks in Your Montana Garden? The Rise of Praying Mantises - NewsBreak
text:
By Michael Foth ,
4 hours ago Manitis ‚Äì Credit Canva/Kolleen Waldo, used with permission Facebook can get pretty annoying. Sometimes I want to delete the app and my account soooo badly. I feel like if social media disappeared tomorrow, perhaps the world would be a slightly better place.
For my line of work, however, it‚Äôs a bit of a necessity. And despite all the targeted ads, divisive political arguments, AI slop, and doom-scrolling¬†in the Comments, there are a few local pages I like to follow. One of them is Ask Billings .
The page is relatively drama and troll-free and is basically exactly what it sounds like. Questions about Billings. ‚ÄúWhat was this building? Where can I find in Billings? Who has the best in Billings?‚Äù You get the idea.
Credit Kolleen Waldo via Facebook, used with permission What is this strange thing? Recently, someone posted a picture (seen above), wondering what the item in the photo is. My initial guess was some kind of dauber-type bug nest. I was close , but wrong. The thing pictured is a cocoon-like bundle of praying mantis eggs. The internet says,
Praying mantis eggs are enclosed in a protective, foamy, Styrofoam-like casing known as an ootheca (plural: oothecae ). These cases are laid by the female in late summer or fall on twigs or stems to protect the developing nymphs through winter.
Credit Kolleen Waldo, used with permission Don‚Äôt mess with the ootheca. You shouldn‚Äôt¬†remove the egg sacs unless you have an issue with an interesting, cute, and beneficial insect. Praying mantises ( alternate¬†plural: mantids or mantes ) have a ravenous appetite for (mostly) bad bugs in your garden.
Download the KCTR Mobile App Now According to the Green Bay Botanical Center , praying mantises will devour ‚Äúmosquitoes, mites, moths, wasps, flies, cockroaches, and many more insects.‚Äù They don‚Äôt seem to discriminate, though‚Ä¶ they‚Äôll also eat butterflies, bees, and spiders;¬†larger¬†mantises have been known to eat small frogs or minnows. Who knew?
Praying mantis ‚Äì Photo by William Warby on Unsplash Are praying mantises becoming more common in Montana? I‚Äôve lived here since 1988, and I don‚Äôt recall seeing praying mantises in our yard or garden very often ‚Äì if ever ‚Äì until the last decade or so. We now see a few each summer here in the Billings area.
I‚Äôll typically find one in my garden plot, but sometimes we‚Äôll see one on the window screens. They‚Äôre¬†usually bright green, and I‚Äôve never seen them get bigger than maybe 4 ‚Äì 5 inches long.
My kids love watching them, and I like seeing them in my garden, eating spider mites, aphids, and whatever else they enjoy.¬†They can bite humans, but it‚Äôs reportedly rare, and when handled gently, you should be fine.
If you do get nipped, praying mantises¬†are not venomous and rarely break the skin. Like the dentist says, ‚Äúit‚Äôs just a little pinch.‚Äù
Are These 12 Bugs That We See In Spring Dangerous? Gallery Credit: Brett Alan Getty Images/iStockphoto Mosquito Believe it or not, mosquitos are one of the most deadly creatures on earth. They carry a ton of disease and can easily spread it through blood. In general, they're just a huge pain in the butt. Their bites can itch for days or weeks. For the most part, they're just a huge nuisance, but it has to be mentioned that they can actually be dangerous.
So how do you avoid them?
Make sure to empty barrels and basins that could have standing water in them Wear long pants with socks and long sleeves Wear insect repellant Watch Video Here Poravute Little Black Ants These are dangerous to your sugar bowl, but as far as being dangerous to you, not so much. They have a stinger, but it's way too small to really affect a human. While they're a huge problem for a lot of people from an invasion perspective, there are tons of natural ways to avoid them setting up shop in your kitchen without using harsh chemicals. Getty Images Cicada Cicada's aren't really dangerous to you. They won't hurt you, They're loud and they're scary to look at. But all in all these ones are probably the least of our worries. (YouTube via eas2edward) Red Lilly Leaf Beatle These bugs won't hurt you but if you have a garden, these can really do some damage to it. They love to eat leaves, stem, buds, and flowers, of lilies and other flowers like them.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JTWghQov1PQ (YouTube via Deep Look) Silverfish These ones might be the creepiest looking insects on the list. But really, if you can handle looking at them, they're not that bad at all. They might cause some damage to clothes that you have stored, or books, but for the most part they won't cause you any problems.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KefMerovEjY (YouTube via Solutions Pest & Lawn) Marmorated Stink Bug How many of these have you already seen? Don't squish them. They stink when you squish them...hence the name. And if you're reading by a light, they might dive bomb you by accident. It has nothing to do with you...they just love the lights.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aHiLSeS8l3s (YouTube via Modern Pest Services) Cluster Fly These are not quite the same as house flies. They lay their eggs in the ground outside and when it gets warmer out will come into your house for protection. They aren't known to bite or carry any disease. The problem comes from the fact that you will get so many of them all at once. When you get cluster flies, you'll get hundreds or thousands of them at a time.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KVTHDXwcUtE (YouTube via Fabricio Mart) Crane Fly These look worse than they are. They look like enormous mosquitos. But they don't actually bite. Some people call them mosquito hawks although they don't actually eat mosquitos. Adult crane flies don't eat at all! But young crane flies will eat dead plant material.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FNnS_yzQ3tg (YouTube via Nature at Your Door Frank Taylor) Asian lady beetle or Japanese lady bug These ones look like lady bugs...only they're orange. The good news is that they prey on pests that will destroy our gardens. The bad news is that they're a huge nuisance themselves. They can bite and be aggressive, are harmful to dogs, invade your home, and leave behind a foul-smelling yellowish secretion that can stain walls and furniture. They multiply quickly too. So try to keep them outside if you can. Make sure your windows stay closed or at the very least that your screens are in good shape.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PkfLvONwYjc (YouTube via Insects Limited) Fruit Fly How many times have you run into these things already this spring? The biggest problem with fruit flies are the bacteria and germs that they carry with them. They're difficult to get rid of without professional help.
https://youtu.be/WJ75QeNViog (YouTube via CMU LMDC) Caddisfly These are the insects that most fly fishermen create their "flies" to look like when hitting a stream because that's where they come from. The larvae are aquatic, but the adults live above water. The problem with them is how they swarm areas. You'll find them around lights all summer long. They aren't dangerous to humans. They can just be annoying.
